source.title: Scaling Laws for Discriminative Speech Recognition Rescoring Models
source.authors: Yi-Le Gu; Prashanth Gurunath Shivakumar; J. Kolehmainen; Ankur Gandhe; A. Rastrow; I. Bulyko

record.file_problem: Full paper text is present. PDF extraction has some layout and equation formatting artifacts; values visible only in figures are not text-extracted.
record.tranche_reason: Tests whether scaling relationships apply in a new setting: discriminative speech-recognition rescoring, including models fine-tuned from pretraining.
record.gate_note: The paper reports its own WER scaling fits and explicit comparisons. The figures contain additional plotted measurements, but their individual WER values are not available in the extracted text. Cited scaling results from other papers are not recorded as rows.
record.test_reason: The study fits its own power laws for normalized WER of BERT-based speech rescorers against discriminative training data and model size. It covers both scratch and pretrained-then-fine-tuned models. That is a new setting and transfer regime for the scaling-law form (V5), and a downstream-task metric scaling with pretrained model size (V6).
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly correct. The authors also state the laws hold over two orders of magnitude and expect the data-limited regime to typify most speech-recognition applications. They caution that the laws break down at extreme data sizes and would need modification once scratch models are not data-limited.
record.recipe_differences: Applies scaling analysis to WERnorm in discriminative speech-recognition rescoring, rather than held-out language-model cross-entropy loss. It studies scratch and pretrained models and does not test compute-optimal allocation.
record.method_sensitivity: The observed relationship depends on whether models are trained from scratch or fine-tuned from pretrained models; scratch-model size has no reported effect in the studied data-limited regime, whereas pretrained-model size does.
record.problems: The study uses internal English data and reports no uncertainty estimates. The authors note that the tested scratch models are in a data-limited regime and that scaling laws may break down at extreme data sizes. Individual figure-point values are not available in the extracted text.
record.rows_left_out: Individual plotted WERnorm values by model size and training-data point in Figures 2 and 3 were not entered separately because their numeric values are not text-extracted. The reported fit parameters and explicit textual comparisons are recorded instead.

untested.parts: Pretraining loss is not measured; the outcome is downstream WERnorm.
No extrapolation test: fits are made on all runs, with no held-out larger runs.
No compute budget or compute-optimal allocation.
Model shape is not varied at a fixed parameter count.
Only speech rescoring with MWER fine-tuning is covered. Image/video models and repeated data are not tested.
No prediction from pretraining loss. Only one task and four model sizes; pretraining tokens are not varied.
Fitting method, parameter counting, schedule and data are not varied. The study does not compare its exponents with other published fits.

record.verdict_notes: Interspeech paper on internal Amazon data with no uncertainty reported. The exponents are very small and WERnorm varies only over about 0.8–1.0, so the power-law fit is weakly constrained. Data units (hours vs utterances) are ambiguous in the text. The reader's V7 links are dropped: comparing scratch with pretrained is a regime difference, not a fitting-choice dependence.

versions.untested_parts: The measured outcome is normalized word error rate (WERnorm) for speech rescoring, not held-out pretraining loss of language models.
The study fits its reported relationships to the studied runs, but does not report a test in which fits from small runs predict runs orders of magnitude larger.
No fixed-compute-budget comparison or compute-optimal allocation between parameters and tokens is tested.
The study varies model size but does not compare depth, width, or other architecture details at a fixed parameter count.
Tests speech-recognition rescoring with discriminative training and pretraining transfer, not image or video models, repeated-data training, or other fine-tuning and transfer settings.
Tests WER for speech-recognition rescoring, not a range of downstream task families or prediction from pretraining loss.

Compares scratch and pretrained rescoring settings and discusses limits of applicability, but does not vary parameter-count conventions, fitting methods, or training schedules, nor compare against other studies' fits.

rows.subject: RescoreBERT models trained from scratch (5M, 17M, 170M, 700M)
rows.operation_detail: Fit normalized WER against discriminative training-data size across the reported model sizes.

conditions.value: 300 to 95300 (figure axis; text identifies 95300 training utterances)

rows.value: Power-law fit: WERnorm = (DC/D)^αD; DC = 8.82 and αD = 0.0146. Authors state WERnorm has a power-law relationship with training data and is independent of model size in this regime.
rows.note: Reported fit describes the tested data-limited regime; the individual plotted WERnorm values are not text-extracted.
rows.check: V5 only: scratch models have no pretraining, so this is not downstream predictability (V6), and no fitting choice is varied (V7). Data units are inconsistent: the text says 95300 'of' training data and the figure axis says hours, while the record says utterances. The fit covers 300–95300 with a tiny exponent (αD=0.0146), so WERnorm spans only about 0.8–1.0.

source_check.correct: Training-data range: 300–95300, labeled hours in the figures. Section 2.3 has malformed unit wording and does not establish 95300 utterances.
source_check.locator_found: Section 2.3; Figure 2 axes; Figure 3 legend; Section 3.2, Equation (7).
source_check.problem: The condition asserts an utterance count despite inconsistent source units.

rows.subject: RescoreBERT models fine-tuned from pre-trained models (5M, 17M, 170M, 700M)
rows.operation_detail: Fit normalized WER as a function of discriminative training-data size and model size.

conditions.value: 300 to 95300 (figure axis; text identifies 95300 training utterances)
MLM on Wikipedia and mC4, then internal catalog data; up to around 1 trillion tokens in total

rows.value: Power-law fit: WERnorm = (DC/(kD^αN^β))^αD, with DC = 8.82, αD = 0.0146, k = 2.27 × 10^-11, α = 1.71, and β = 1.24. Authors state the fit captures the data and WER decreases with increasing model size.
rows.note: The paper states the fit parameters and describes its fit as capturing the data; individual plotted WERnorm values are not text-extracted.
rows.check: Remove V7: no fitting method, parameter convention or schedule is varied. Eq. 8 reuses DC and αD from the scratch fit, so only k, α and β are fitted to pretrained runs. The paper says the fit 'captures the data well' but gives no goodness-of-fit numbers or uncertainty.

source_check.correct: Training-data range: 300–95300, labeled hours in the figures; the utterance-count interpretation is not established. Equation (8): DC=8.82, αD=0.0146, k=2.27×10^-11, α=1.71, β=1.24.
source_check.locator_found: Section 2.3; Figure 2 axes; Figure 3 legend; Section 3.3, Equation (8).
source_check.problem: The condition asserts an utterance count despite inconsistent source units.

rows.subject: RescoreBERT, 5M model
rows.stage_stated: trained from scratch versus fine-tuned from a pre-trained model
rows.operation_detail: Compare the data required by scratch and pretrained models to reach the same WERnorm.
rows.note: The authors give this as an example of the data reduction associated with pretraining.
rows.check: This is an illustrative read-off from Figure 2 (about 30k vs about 1k) on data efficiency from transfer. It bears on the transfer regime (V5), not on downstream predictability or fit-dependence. Remove V6 and V7.

source_check.locator_found: Section 3.3, example preceding the effective-transfer formulation.

rows.subject: RescoreBERT models trained from scratch (5M, 17M, 170M, 700M)
rows.operation_detail: Report the relationship between model size and WERnorm in the tested data regime.

conditions.value: the amount used in this study, up to 95300 training utterances

rows.measure: Effect of model size on WERnorm
rows.value: Authors state WERnorm is independent of model size in this regime and that the regime is limited by training data.
rows.note: The authors expect model size to begin influencing WERnorm for scratch models if training data is increased sufficiently; they say the scaling laws would then likely need modification.
rows.check: No parameter scaling for scratch models. This is consistent with the claim's 'other factors not the bottleneck' clause, since the authors say these models are data-limited. Remove V6 (no pretraining) and V7.

source_check.correct: Studied data-limited regime: training-data sizes up to 95300, labeled hours in the figures; 95300 utterances is not established.
source_check.problem: The condition presents the ambiguously reported training-data quantity as an utterance count.

rows.subject: RescoreBERT models fine-tuned from pre-trained models (5M, 17M, 170M, 700M)
rows.operation_detail: Report how model size relates to WERnorm after fine-tuning.

conditions.value: the amounts studied, up to 95300 training utterances

rows.measure: Effect of model size on WERnorm
rows.value: Authors state that larger pretrained models lead to more improvement, unlike scratch models in the tested data-limited regime.
rows.note: The authors attribute the larger-model benefit to better memorizing and leveraging pretraining knowledge.
rows.check: Remove V7. This is a qualitative statement from Figure 3(b); no per-size values are extracted.

rows.subject: RescoreBERT models fine-tuned from pre-trained models
rows.operation_detail: Estimate the effective data transferred from pretraining and fit its relationship to fine-tuning data and model size.

conditions.value: pretraining and fine-tuning use different training objectives

rows.value: The paper applies DT = kD^αN^β, with k = 2.27 × 10^-11, α = 1.71, and β = 1.24; it states that a 10x increase in model size is worth approximately a 5.3x increase in data size.
rows.note: The authors describe this as consistent with prior work on transfer scaling and report that it also holds here despite the different pretraining and fine-tuning objectives.
rows.check: DT is not measured separately; it is inferred through the Eq. 8 fit, and its parameters duplicate R2's. Remove V7. The 5.3x figure follows from 10^(β/α)=10^0.725.

relationships.condition: BERT rescorers, scratch and pretrained, 300–95300 training data, 5M–700M parameters
relationships.reason: WERnorm fits power laws in data (scratch) and in data and size (pretrained), and transferred data follows a power-law form (R1, R2, R3, R6).
relationships.display_finding: Normalized word error rate followed data power laws from scratch and joint data–size power laws after pretraining, while transferred data also followed a power law.

relationships.condition: Randomly initialized rescorers in the studied data-limited regime
relationships.reason: No parameter scaling for scratch models (R4); the authors attribute this to the data bottleneck and expect the laws to need modification with more data.
relationships.display_finding: Increasing parameters did not improve randomly initialized rescorers, which the authors attributed to a data bottleneck.

source_check.label: limits_scope
source_check.condition: Randomly initialized rescorers in the studied data-limited regime
source_check.reason: R4's absent parameter-size benefit under a data bottleneck is consistent with the original scaling law's non-bottleneck qualification. Scratch models still follow the data power law; this result does not establish a qualification of V5.

relationships.condition: Pretrained BERT rescorers fine-tuned with MWER loss, 5M–700M
relationships.reason: Downstream WERnorm falls with pretrained model size and is described by the Eq. 8 power law (R2, R5). There are no fit-error numbers.
relationships.display_finding: Normalized word error rate decreased with pretrained model size according to a reported power law, without numerical fit errors.
